creators.name: Jake Thomas
creators.why: The most useful email you get. Each week: 5 titles that beat their channel's average (with the multiple), the formula behind each, why it works, two examples, and a Flop of the Week with fixes. It's your Packaging Lab, delivered.
creators.best: It's Boring, But It Builds An Athletic Physique: 59.5x its channel's average.
creators.watch: Plugs its own tools (title analyzer, outlier finder) in the middle, but they're free to try.

creators.name: Colin & Samir
creators.why: Short Sunday notes from Samir about what makes work matter. The one I read is the best single idea in your inbox about why things get shared.
creators.best: The question I ask everyone: work breaks into culture when people can see themselves in it.
creators.watch: Some weeks are just episode promos.

creators.name: Anne-Laure Le Cunff
creators.why: A neuroscientist writing about curiosity and how to run your life as small experiments. Sources linked, ideas you can try in a week.
creators.best: Algorithmic Resistance: why feeds make everyone's taste the same, and small ways to discover things yourself.
creators.watch: The bottom half is community events and sponsors. Stop at 'Brain Picks'.

creators.name: James Clear
creators.why: Three short ideas, two quotes, one question. Takes 2 minutes and is usually worth it.
creators.best: Skill comes before results, practice before skill, attitude before practice. And: when stuck, ask 'What can I do?'
creators.watch: The book ads at the bottom are long.

creators.name: Jon Youshaei
creators.why: Ex-YouTube/Instagram marketer. Wednesday: creator-economy news, best thumbnails of the week, and one outlier broken down. Sunday: a story or tip.
creators.best: Weekly Outlier: a 26M-view video (31x average) explained in three points: double-take thumbnail, instant premise, real stakes.
creators.watch: Sunday 'comics' are lighter. Free Discord with 7,000 creators for feedback.

creators.name: Ali Abdaal
creators.why: Friendly, personal notes from the doctor-turned-YouTuber. Light on ideas, but each has one useful question.
creators.best: My new morning routine: is there an hour you spend by default that you'd enjoy more elsewhere in the day?
creators.watch: Sponsored section plus course plugs.

creators.name: Jay Clouse
creators.why: How full-time creators run their business: teams, launches, memberships. Smart, but mostly for later.
creators.best: Six-week sprints: one theme, go all in, learn, repeat.
creators.watch: Long, with a sponsor block. Jay is on paternity leave, so the team writes it.

creators.name: Aprilynne Alter
creators.why: One of the sharpest YouTube strategists (she's already in your Intro Lab). Only the welcome email so far, so give it a month.
creators.best: (Only the welcome so far.)
creators.watch: Sponsored by 1of10, so expect some tool plugs.

creators.name: Editor Josh
creators.why: Will Tennyson's main editor. Mostly course sales, but there's a real opportunity in here: he re-edits subscribers' videos on camera.
creators.best: Can I re-edit your video? Send a recent, decent edit, not your masterpiece.
creators.watch: Case-study sales emails every other day.

creators.name: Bryan Ng
creators.why: Script coach for big personal brands. Honest, but most emails just point to his latest video.
creators.best: I hate my YouTube channel but make $100k a month: only 17 uploads in 10 months.

creators.name: Dr Rupy Aujla
creators.why: A doctor with a nutrition master's. Credible but basic: whole foods, fibre, sleep, stress. Most emails sell his recipe app.
creators.best: The 5 practices: cook from scratch, eat a variety of plants, move daily, sleep, wind down.
creators.watch: App@ emails are pure promos.

creators.name: Nik
creators.why: Three book summaries a week, gently written. Good for finding books, not for your channel.
creators.best: Alan Watts, The Wisdom of Insecurity: if you have an identity crisis, maybe you think you only have one identity.

creators.name: Clark Kegley
creators.why: Self-improvement YouTuber. The welcome email is a list of his best videos, which is a useful packaging reference for your niche.
creators.best: This helped 1M people: titles like 'I read 300 self-improvement books to learn these 3 lessons'.
creators.watch: Sells a journaling course.

creators.name: JAWLINER
creators.why: Pure promos, but useful for your gum video: their before/after photos and claims ('visible results after a few weeks') are perfect material to fact-check on camera.
creators.best: 'These people took the exercises seriously': before/afters with different lighting, angles and colour.
creators.watch: Unsubscribe after you've saved what you need for the gum video.

creators.name: Tico
creators.why: Story of a Miami kid hired by iShowSpeed at 16. One good line ('your camera is fine'), then a pitch. The sender name shows as 'Juliyan', which is a sketchy trick.
creators.best: You DON'T need better gear: he shot NBA games with a borrowed camera.
creators.watch: Sender name is spoofed to look like you.

creators.name: Tool companies
creators.why: 1of10 and Subscribr are useful tools, but their emails are webinar and launch funnels. Viewstats sends picture-only charts. SPI is selling a Black Friday lifetime deal.
creators.best: Subscribr's one good idea: build the thumbnail first, then the title.

creators.name: QOVES
creators.why: Sells AI 'biometric scores' and glow-up protocols. Same niche as you, opposite approach. No evidence in the emails.
creators.best: (none)

creators.name: Andrew Tate
creators.why: Shame as motivation ('you have failed everyone who ever loved you'). No ideas, no evidence. The opposite of your brand: help the viewer, never trade trust.
creators.best: (none)

creators.name: Adam Mastroianni
creators.why: The best thinker in your inbox. A psychologist who shows how studies fail, in funny, sharp writing. Every issue makes you better at judging the evidence your channel is built on.
creators.best: We need more goat sacrifices: most big programs meant to change people have zero measured effect, and one-off studies are worth little.
creators.watch: Long reads (15+ min). Save them for the weekend.

creators.name: Ed Lawrence
creators.why: Real numbers from someone who has made millions on YouTube: views vs money, ideation, scripts, pivots. Written for coaches who sell courses, so half of it is about funnels you don't have yet.
creators.best: 100 nuggets of YouTube wisdom: the list he wishes he'd had in 2019.
creators.watch: Two sender addresses (film-booth.com and story-os.ai) = double the emails. Every P.S. sells Story OS.

creators.name: Antonio
creators.why: A weekly digest of what's over-performing: title formats, hooks pulled from outliers, thumbnail styles, and a 'twist' for each niche. The niches are rarely yours, but the patterns transfer.
creators.best: 6 thumbnails that work in any niche: Downfall and Comparison grids pulled from outlier videos.
creators.watch: It exists to sell the TubeLab tool. Skip the 'welcome' and 'last day for your code' emails.

creators.name: rystal
creators.why: Short emails, one idea each, all about getting better at Resolve and Fusion. The taste + 15-minute loop is exactly the kind of small daily rep you like.
creators.best: stop being bad at editing: taste is the bottleneck, not your PC.
creators.watch: The 30-day course ended in September. Now it's mostly TypeFlow update emails.

creators.name: Marcus Jones
creators.why: Friendly Saturday essays on motivation and follow-through. Mostly ideas you already know from books (room for error, tribes, crabs in a bucket). Aimed at gaming creators.
creators.best: Some life-changing ideas for ya: tribes, learning from other fields, room for error.
creators.watch: Comes as HTML only, so it often looks empty in previews.

creators.name: Mark Tilbury
creators.why: Kind, simple money basics (start now, time is the scarce thing, don't only sell hours). Nothing you'll act on this year.
creators.best: What rich people figured out about time: the 86,400-seconds idea.
creators.watch: Only a few emails a year.

creators.name: chicgirlmoment
creators.why: Opinions and personal observations, no sources, written for young women. One good idea (park what fascinates you on a list) per many emails.
creators.best: 12 ways to ruin your brain: multitasking two thinking tasks, phone first and last thing, bed as an office.
creators.watch: Half of each post is paywalled.

creators.name: Love Made Logical
creators.why: Ads written to look like a newsletter. Worth keeping one as a case study: it's a textbook looks-niche affiliate funnel (celebrity hairline → Norwood scale → personal story → discount code).
creators.best: Have you seen Tom Cruise lately?: a minoxidil + derma-pen ad.
creators.watch: Overclaims what minoxidil can do. See the deep dive.

creators.name: The Builders
creators.why: Just promos for podcast episodes. Watch the episodes on YouTube if a guest interests you.
creators.best: Alex Karp on the surveillance state.

creators.name: Hamza Ahmed
creators.why: Last email was 2023, a teaser for a video. Nothing left to read.
creators.best: Any plans this weekend?

creators.name: Editing shops
creators.by: Video Editor Studio, sh4rk, European Filmmaker, X-Session, Creative Herd
creators.why: Pure sales: discounts, launches, 'last 48 hours'. Unsubscribing would remove about a third of your creator mail.
creators.best: (none worth reading)

ideas.title: 'It's Boring, But It Works': 59.5x
ideas.body: 'It's Boring, But It Builds An Athletic Physique' did 59.5x its channel's average, the biggest outlier in your whole inbox. Boring vs a result you want is a strong contrast, and 'it' opens a loop.
ideas.use: 'It's Boring, But It Fixed My Skin' or 'It's Boring, But It Got Rid of My Puffy Face'. Only if the method really is boring and really worked.

ideas.title: 'Which X Are Actually Worth It? (Tier List)': 15.5x
ideas.body: A question plus 'actually' (which challenges what people believe) plus a tier list. Farm animals did 15.5x.
ideas.use: 'Which Skincare Products Are Actually Worth It? (Tier List)'. Your evidence ranking is the tier list, and that's your edge over everyone else.

ideas.title: Good thing, bad result
ideas.body: 'Why "Good Parenting" Creates Clingy Kids' (8.4x), 'The Hidden Trap of Working Hard' (4.4x), 'Stop Drawing Perfect Lines: A Better Way to Sketch' (11x). A habit people think is good leads to a result they don't want.
ideas.use: 'Why "Clean Eating" Can Make You Look Bloated', 'Stop Mewing: A Better Way to a Sharper Jaw'. Make sure the science backs the twist.

ideas.title: '(Most People Are Level 1)': 8.5x
ideas.body: 'The Ultimate Guide to Social Intelligence (Most People Are Level 1)'. Status: everyone wants to know their level. Jake says the very specific thumbnail did half the work.
ideas.use: 'The Ultimate Guide to Looking Good (Most Guys Are Level 1)'. A levels ladder (1-5) is also a perfect visual for your wojaks.

ideas.title: Simple titles win, same channel
ideas.body: Same guitar channel: 'Slash's Stupidly Simple Techniques for EPIC Solos' got 205K views, 'Slash's GENIUS Approach to using Minor Pentatonic in Major Keys' got 5.8K. And '7 Gym Hacks Every Lifter Should Know' flopped (0.18x): no benefit promised.
ideas.use: Before publishing, check: does the title promise a result a 15-year-old understands in 1 second? Jargon ('retinoids', 'masseter') goes in the video, not the title.

ideas.title: Check the keyword before you film
ideas.body: A video titled around 'boundaries' flopped (0.17x). Searching that word in an outlier tool showed almost no videos with it ever beat their average. People just don't click it.
ideas.use: Before scripting, search your main word (e.g. 'debloat', 'mewing', 'skincare routine') in your Packaging Lab or an outlier tool. No outliers = rethink the angle.

ideas.title: Proven topic + borrowed format = original
ideas.body: Take topics that work in your niche, and formats that work outside it (in channels with a similar style). The mix is both proven and original.
ideas.use: Topic: debloating (works in your niche). Format: 'I tried X for 30 days, what did it really cost?' (travel/finance). Result: 'I Debloated For 30 Days: What Did It Really Cost?'

ideas.title: People share what they see themselves in
ideas.body: Samir asked director Petra Collins the difference between views and culture: 'If people can see themselves in the work.' The work isn't to be louder, it's to be truer, so that someone thinks 'I feel that too'. That person shares it.
ideas.use: For every video, write the one 'I feel that too' sentence your viewer would say. If you can't, the video is information, not connection.

ideas.title: Algorithms make everyone the same
ideas.body: Over 75% of YouTube watch time came from recommendations (YouTube, 2018). When feeds reward the same formats, creators copy them and culture gets more uniform. Anne-Laure's fix: little acts of 'algorithmic resistance', like full albums, library books and recommendations from friends.
ideas.use: Your taste is your edge. Get some inputs from outside the feed (books, people, your own tests), or your videos will look like everyone else's.

ideas.title: 'I will [X] for [2 weeks]'
ideas.body: Ness Labs turns every idea into a tiny experiment with one fill-in-the-blank sentence and a time limit. It's not a habit forever, just a test you review at the end.
ideas.use: This is literally your channel format. Say the sentence on camera at the start of each test video: 'I will chew this gum 1 hour a day for 60 days.'

ideas.title: Attitude, then practice, then skill, then results
ideas.body: James Clear: everyone wants results. Skill comes before results, practice before skill, and attitude (being willing to keep trying) before practice. When stuck, ask: 'What can I do?'
ideas.use: When a video flops, don't judge the result, judge the practice: did you do your reps (scripts, packaging reviews) this week?

ideas.title: Swap one default hour
ideas.body: Ali moved an hour of late-night scrolling to a 7am walk with an audiobook. Same hour, much better use. He also started with a rough version and fixed the annoying bits as he went, instead of planning the perfect routine.
ideas.use: Find one default hour (probably phone at night) and swap it into your Life OS: filming, reading, or the gym.

ideas.title: Run your channel in 6-week sprints
ideas.body: Creator Science works in six-week sprints: one theme per cycle (e.g. 'best launch ever', 'members never want to leave'), lots of experiments, then a review.
ideas.use: Next 6 weeks: one theme only, e.g. 'packaging': every video gets 3 thumbnails and a keyword check. Review on week 6.

ideas.title: A free thumbnail A/B test log
ideas.body: Chewbr (a small tool maker in your inbox) sent a free Google Sheet to log thumbnail swaps: what you changed, when, and the before/after numbers. Otherwise you never know if the swap caused the change.
ideas.use: Use YouTube's built-in Test & Compare for every video and log the result. After 10 tests you'll have your own thumbnail rules.

ideas.title: Free pro feedback on your edit
ideas.body: Editor Josh (Will Tennyson's editor) asked subscribers to send a recent, decent edit, and he'll re-edit parts of it on camera, explaining the pacing, music and shot choices.
ideas.use: Send one of your videos via the form in his 27 Oct email. Worst case: nothing. Best case: free expert notes plus exposure on his channel.

ideas.title: Does this moment move the story?
ideas.body: Josh's one-question edit: for each moment, ask 'How does this move the story forward?' If it doesn't, cut it. If it strengthens it, highlight it (zoom, music, text).
ideas.use: Do one pass of your next timeline asking only this question. It's faster than any effect pack.

ideas.title: Double-take, instant premise, real stakes
ideas.body: Jon's outlier of the week (26M views, 31x): a thumbnail that makes you look twice (a stretched car), a premise you get in a second ('widest street-legal car'), and real stakes ('street legal', so can it actually drive?).
ideas.use: Check your gum thumbnail against all three: does it make me look twice? Do I get it in 1 second? Is there something at stake?

ideas.title: Instagram's $500K checks won't last
ideas.body: Instagram is reportedly paying creators $50K-500K to post long videos, and not asking for exclusivity. It paid up to $250K for IGTV in 2019, and IGTV was shut down by 2022. YouTube's revenue share has paid creators over $100B since 2021.
ideas.use: Build on the platform that pays per view forever (YouTube). Repost to Instagram for free reach, but don't plan around platform bonuses.

ideas.title: Before/afters are mostly photography
ideas.body: The JAWLINER emails in your inbox (you've bought from them) show 'before/afters' with different light, angles, colour, haircuts and clenched jaws. Their FAQ says most customers see results 'after only a few weeks'. That's very fast for a muscle to visibly grow.
ideas.use: Make 'spot the trick' a segment of your gum video, then show your own photos taken under the same conditions. Honesty is the hook.

ideas.title: Shame isn't motivation
ideas.body: Andrew Tate's emails say things like 'You are unhappy because you have failed everyone who ever loved you.' Shame might get a click, but it destroys trust and teaches nothing.
ideas.use: Your anti-model. When a hook works by making the viewer feel worthless, rewrite it so the viewer feels capable instead.

ideas.title: Your camera is fine
ideas.body: Tico shot NBA games with a borrowed camera. rystal (old inbox) says the same about editing PCs: the gap is taste and what you do after you shoot, not the gear.
ideas.use: Before buying anything for Black Friday, ask: will this fix my biggest weakness? Usually that's packaging or scripting, not kit.

ideas.title: Build a flywheel, not a launch
ideas.body: Big results come from many small pushes on one loop, each turn feeding the next (Jim Collins). Ed's version: every video promotes something, the email list grows, money funds better videos.
ideas.use: Your loop: honest test video → right viewers → their comments → better ideas and proof → next video. Upload rhythm is the push.

ideas.title: Give away the free version of your system
ideas.body: Ed put his paid program's basic version in one video ('$0 to $1M, step by step'): 1-3 simple actions per step, then a call to action. He says it made $240k in 90 days. His mistake: he mentioned his email list at minute 19 instead of the first 90 seconds.
ideas.use: Your version later: 'My whole glow-up system in one video'. It works as a binge video now and a funnel once you sell something.

ideas.title: Same views, 20x the money
ideas.body: Ed tracked 198 channels: the top 25% of earners got about the same views per video as the bottom 25% but made ~20x more per view. They make content for buyers and have an offer that's hard to refuse.
ideas.use: Not for now. When sponsors come: one product that solves the same problem as the video beats random deals.

ideas.title: 'Self-improvement' searches are down 45%
ideas.body: Ed looked at 44 course-creator niches: 42 shrank since 2023. Self-improvement -45%, investing -43%. YouTube as a whole is growing.
ideas.use: A reason to stay specific (looks, skin, debloat with science) and not drift into general 'improve your life' videos.

ideas.title: The twist: same format, new audience
ideas.body: Every TubeLab niche ends with a 'twist': take a format that's working and move it to another country, age or room. 'Why orcas fear…' was flooded in English. A French channel did it early and got 1.1M views in 24 days.
ideas.use: Steal the shape, keep your science: 'X grooming rules Korean men follow (and which ones the research backs)'.

ideas.title: 3 hooks that keep showing up in outliers
ideas.body: Cold open (one person, a name, a number, then the twist). 'You' scenario (put the viewer in a moment they know too well; strongest for money, health, fitness). Bold claim (one sentence that sounds wrong, the video proves it).
ideas.use: Your Intro Lab already measured that promise-first openings win. See the deep dive for gum-video versions of each.

ideas.title: 'Finish this sentence…'
ideas.body: An outlier that did 10x its channel average opened with: 'Finish this sentence. I'll finally be happy when…' It makes the viewer answer in their head in the first second.
ideas.use: 'Finish this sentence: I'd look better if my ___ was different.' Then make the video about the most common answer.

ideas.title: The villain is your inner voice
ideas.body: A self-improvement cartoon channel makes wordless animated shorts where the bad guy is the viewer's own inner voice. TubeLab estimates ~6M views across 13 videos.
ideas.use: You already have wojaks. An 'inner voice' wojak arguing with you on screen is a cheap way to show temptation (skipping skincare, junk food).

ideas.title: Steal concepts, not work
ideas.body: rystal says 99% of his ideas are copied concepts: the timing, the easing, the way a title reveals. Surround yourself with work you love, take it apart, then mash several stolen pieces together with your own twist.
ideas.use: Keep a 'steal file' folder: 10-second clips of moves you love, each with one line on what makes it work.

ideas.title: Taste is the bottleneck, not your PC
ideas.body: You can't edit better than what you've seen. Find one editor whose work embarrasses you, frame-step it, replay a moment 25 times, then spend just 15 minutes in Resolve making something.
ideas.use: A 15-minute daily rep that fits your Life OS. Four-week plan in the deep dive.

ideas.title: Leave the script for 2 weeks
ideas.body: Write it, forget it, then edit. You won't remember what you meant, so the weak parts jump out. He also says editing a script should take longer than writing it.
ideas.use: Works with your idea bank: script video N+2 while filming video N, so every script gets a cold read.

ideas.title: 10x more time on ideas than you think
ideas.body: From Ed's 100 nuggets: spend far more time on ideation, do titles and thumbnails first, make several thumbnails, use the community tab to test ideas, and views per video matter more than subscribers.
ideas.use: Matches your packaging-review skill: no script until the title and thumbnail pass.

ideas.title: Buddy up with a creator your size
ideas.body: Meet one creator at a similar level every 2-4 weeks. Share what's working, fix each other's problems. He says this beat anything the internet taught him.
ideas.use: One call a month with a looks or self-improvement creator around your size. Swap thumbnails before posting.

ideas.title: Your viewers grow up with you
ideas.body: Charlie from Charisma on Command (7M subs) is pivoting after 10 years because he's outgrown his topic. His point: long-time viewers changed too, so many want the new topic more. Ed saw the same when he left Film Booth's old topic.
ideas.use: When you move to the Netherlands and uni, your audience can come along. Don't force topics you've outgrown, viewers can tell.

ideas.title: The Iron Law: most interventions do nothing
ideas.body: Sociologist Peter Rossi (1987): the expected effect of a big social program is zero, and the better the evaluation, the more likely it finds nothing. Laptops for every child in Peru: a 10-year trial of 531 schools found no effect on grades.
ideas.use: Your channel's edge is saying 'this doesn't work' honestly. Tiny tricks promising big changes (mewing, gum, cold water) need big evidence.

ideas.title: Bad study, real effect
ideas.body: The famous 1975 'illusion of control' study gave people football cards, not lottery tickets. People who picked chose their favourite players, so of course they valued them more. Proper replications with real lotteries find nothing. Yet superstitions are everywhere, so the feeling is real.
ideas.use: A great script move: 'The famous study is wrong… but the thing it describes is real.' Viewers love being let in on it.

ideas.title: Ask 'how could I 10x?' every year
ideas.body: Ed asked each January what could 10x his business, then tried and failed. Failing at 10x still doubled it 4 years in a row. Idea from the book '10x Is Easier Than 2x' (Sullivan & Hardy).
ideas.use: For your yearly review: 2x thinking means 'upload a bit more'. 10x thinking forces a different system (editor, batching, a format that travels).

ideas.title: 86,400 seconds
ideas.body: If someone stole $10 from your $86,400, you wouldn't throw away the rest. You get 86,400 seconds a day, so don't let 10 bad seconds wreck the other 86,390.
ideas.use: A quick reset line for a bad comment or a flop video.

ideas.title: Park what fascinates you
ideas.body: When a new idea grabs you but it's not the time, write it on a list instead of starting it. Your brain stops nagging you once it knows the idea is saved.
ideas.use: Your idea bank already does this. Add a 'later, not never' section for non-YouTube projects (games, apps).

ideas.title: How a looks-niche ad is built
ideas.body: Celebrity comparison (Tom Cruise vs Jude Law hairlines) → a scale you check yourself against (Norwood) → personal 'I was losing it too' story → doctor said it's fine → discount code. Every step is copyable. The claims aren't.
ideas.use: Use the structure honestly when you have a sponsor: comparison, self-check, your real test, then the code, with only claims the studies support.

ideas.title: Minoxidil + microneedling does beat minoxidil alone
ideas.body: Several meta-analyses of small trials find that adding microneedling to minoxidil gives more hair than minoxidil alone, and one network analysis ranked the combo top. But 'regrow everything you lost' is ad talk.
ideas.use: A strong evidence-based video for your audience: 'Losing hair at 18: the only 3 things with real evidence'.

ideas.title: Leave room for error
ideas.body: The biggest wins are rare and take time to compound. Whoever can survive a few flops stays in the game long enough to catch one. Marcus borrows this from money writers like Morgan Housel.
ideas.use: Plan your channel so one flop never makes you quit: a buffer of 2 finished videos, school first, no money pressure.

images.title: The jaw 'before / after' split
images.cap: One face, split down the middle: 'no pronounced jaw muscle' vs 'bigger jaw muscle through constant training'. The right half is shot from lower with harder side light.
images.use: Freeze it in your gum video and circle what changed: the light and the angle, not the muscle. Then show your own honest Day 1 vs Day 60.

images.title: Before/after #1: black-and-white vs colour
images.cap: 'Real results. Real persistence.' Before is soft black-and-white with a relaxed face. After is high-contrast, from a slightly lower angle, jaw clenched.
images.use: A 'spot the 4 tricks' moment: colour, contrast, angle, clenching. Viewers love finding them before you reveal them.

images.title: Before/after #2: different everything
images.cap: Different haircut, head tilt, lighting, background and even headphones. Lean-out and grooming could explain much of the difference.
images.use: Use it to set your rules: same light, same distance, same time of day, neutral face, same hair. Show the rules on screen.

images.title: The Downfall thumbnail
images.cap: A fall from greatness: big loss number or a mocking word, red arrow down, high contrast. Each of these beat its channel's average by 5-20x.
images.use: 'The fall of the jawline gum trend' or 'Why mewing is getting exposed', only if the video really tells that story.

images.title: The Comparison thumbnail
images.cap: Split panels with one number each ($2 vs $75). One clear promise: you have to know the difference.
images.use: Perfect for looks: '$4 vs $40 moisturiser', 'Day 1 vs Day 60'. Matches your Thumb Lab finding that outcome thumbnails win (78% hits vs 32%).

images.title: The Norwood scale
images.cap: The 7-stage chart doctors use for male pattern hair loss. The ad used it to make readers check their own hairline.
images.use: A ready-made visual for a hair-loss video: viewers find their own number in 2 seconds (a self-test, which your Intro Lab says is a replay magnet).

deep.title: 12 title formats beating their channel's average, rewritten for you
deep.dek: Everything Creator Hooks sent you in the last month, ranked by outlier score, each with a version for a science-based looks channel.
sources: Creator Hooks, issues of 19 Oct, 26 Oct, 2 Nov and 9 Nov 2026 (outlier scores are Creator Hooks' own numbers)
deep.md:
## How to read this

An outlier score is how many times better a video did than that channel's usual video. 10x means ten times its average. It's the fairest way to compare titles because it removes channel size. These scores are Creator Hooks' numbers, not yours, so treat them as strong hints.

## The 12 formats (chart above)

| Format | Score | Your version |
|---|---|---|
| It's Boring, But It (big result) | 59.5x | It's Boring, But It Fixed My Skin |
| Former (authority): The 5-Second Rule I Use Before (moment) | 22.1x | I Tested 40 Products: The 5-Second Check I Do Before Buying Skincare |
| Which (things) Are Actually Worth It? (Tier List) | 15.5x | Which Grooming Products Are Actually Worth It? (Tier List) |
| (Authority)'s Stupidly Simple Techniques for EPIC (thing) | 14.7x | Models' Stupidly Simple Tricks for EPIC Photos |
| Stop (good habit): A Better Way to (goal) | 11.0x | Stop Mewing: A Better Way to a Sharper Jaw |
| The (thing) Crisis Just Took an Unexpected Turn | 10.5x | The Looksmaxxing Trend Just Took an Unexpected Turn |
| We (did X) for (time) - What Did It Really Cost? | 9.2x | I Glowed Up For 90 Days - What Did It Really Cost? |
| The Ultimate Guide to (subject) (Most People Are Level 1) | 8.5x | The Ultimate Guide to Looking Good (Most Guys Are Level 1) |
| Why "Good (habit)" Creates (bad result) | 8.4x | Why "Healthy Eating" Can Make You Look Bloated |
| The Most Overlooked (thing) Every (group) Needs | 7.7x | The Most Overlooked $5 Product Every Guy Needs |
| The #1 Sign (bad thing is true) | 4.9x | The #1 Sign Your Skincare Is Making Things Worse |
| The Hidden Trap of (good thing) | 4.4x | The Hidden Trap of Drinking More Water |

## The patterns behind them

- **Contrast.** Boring vs great result. Simple vs epic. Good habit vs bad result. Two ideas that shouldn't go together make a gap the brain wants to close.
- **'It' and 'this'.** 'It's boring, but **it**...' opens a loop because the title doesn't say what 'it' is.
- **Authority in front.** 'Former CIA', 'Slash's', 'According to Science'. For you that's measured results and studies, not a fake title.
- **Status.** 'Most people are level 1', 'Signs you're ahead of most…'. Everyone wants to know where they rank.
- **Simplicity.** The same channel got 205K views with 'Stupidly Simple Techniques for EPIC Solos' and 5.8K with 'Minor Pentatonic in Major Keys'.

## The flops are as useful as the hits

- '7 Gym Hacks Every Lifter Should Know' (0.18x): a list, but no benefit. Her hit was 'Why You Don't Look Athletic (Even Though You Lift)'.
- 'Set These Boundaries BEFORE You Retire' (0.17x): the word 'boundaries' almost never gets outliers. Check the keyword before you film.
- 'The One Song That Makes Jam Solos Easy' (0.12x): 'song' doesn't sound like a shortcut. 'Trick' would have.

## The honesty rule

Every one of these works for your channel **only if the video delivers the twist**. 'Stop Mewing' is fine if you show what the evidence says works better. If you can't back the twist with a study or your own test, pick another format. Your brand is that the title is true.

deep.title: Spot the tricks: how jawline before/afters are made
deep.dek: The JAWLINER photos in your inbox, taken apart, plus a checklist for your own honest Day 1 vs Day 60 photos.
sources: Your gum video research pack (60-day jawline gum)
Animal and imaging studies on chewing load and masseter size (no good human trial of gum and jaw appearance found)
deep.md:
## What the emails claim

JAWLINER (you've ordered from them) says the masseter is 'the key to a defined, powerful jawline', that their gum turns 'a flat, undefined jaw into a bold, masculine statement', and that most customers see 'visible results after only a few weeks'. The proof is before/after photos.

## The tricks in their photos

Look at the images in this tab (Images) and count them:

1. **Light.** Before: soft, flat light. After: hard side light that throws a shadow under the jaw. Shadow alone 'creates' a jawline.
2. **Colour.** Before in black-and-white with low contrast, after in colour with high contrast.
3. **Angle.** After shots are taken slightly from below, with the chin forward. The neck stretches and the jaw looks sharper.
4. **Clenching.** A clenched masseter bulges. A relaxed one doesn't. Same muscle, different photo.
5. **Everything else.** Different haircut, background, expression, even headphones. Lost body fat (the biggest real factor) never gets mentioned.

## What the evidence says (honestly)

- The masseter is a muscle, so loading it hard can make it a bit bigger. In animal studies, taking chewing load away shrinks it within a week.
- But no good human trial shows that gum changes how the jaw **looks** in a few weeks. Most of what you see under the ear is **body fat, posture and lighting**, then bone, which gum can't change.
- Too much hard chewing can make the jaw joint (TMJ) sore. Stop if it clicks or hurts.

## Your rules for honest photos

- Same place, same light (no window behind you), same time of day.
- Same camera, same lens, same distance (mark the floor with tape).
- Neutral face, teeth apart, jaw relaxed. Then one clenched shot, labelled.
- Same haircut length, same shirt, same head angle (look at a dot on the wall).
- Weigh yourself too: if you lose fat, say so, because that's probably the real cause.

## How to use it in the video

Open the segment with their photo: 'Find the 4 tricks before I show you.' Pause. Circle them one by one. Then show yours, under the rules above, and say exactly what changed and what didn't. The honest result is the payoff no other jawline video gives.

deep.title: Be truer, not louder
deep.dek: Why some videos get shared and others just get watched: Samir, Petra Collins and Anne-Laure Le Cunff, turned into one question to ask before every upload.
sources: Ed Lawrence, Film Booth, 26 Oct 2026 (old inbox)
deep.md:
## Views vs culture

Samir asks everyone the same question: what's the difference between something that gets a lot of views and something that breaks into culture? Director Petra Collins (Olivia Rodrigo's videos) answered: **'If people can see themselves in the work.'**

His takeaway: the job isn't to be louder, it's to be truer. Say what you actually think, honestly enough that someone stops and thinks 'I feel that too'. That's the person who shares it.

## Why loud and samey stops working

Anne-Laure Le Cunff (a neuroscientist who studies curiosity) points out that most of what we watch is picked by algorithms (over 75% of YouTube watch time, by YouTube's own 2018 number). When feeds reward the same formats, creators copy them, and everything starts to look alike. Your viewers are drowning in identical 'looksmaxxing' videos. The one that feels true stands out because it's rare.

## Two warnings from your inbox

- Bryan Ng, who writes scripts for huge channels, admitted he hates his own channel: it got the leftovers while he worked for others. Doing it for the algorithm alone burns out even the pros.
- Ed Lawrence (old inbox) said his last Film Booth videos were forced, and the views showed it.

## The one question

Before each upload, finish this sentence as your viewer:

> 'I feel that too: ______.'

Examples for your channel:

- Gum video: 'I've also stared at my side profile in a car window and hated it.'
- Debloat video: 'I also wake up looking puffy and don't know why.'
- Skincare: 'I also bought 6 products and have no idea which one works.'

If you can't fill the blank, the video is information. It might still get views, but it won't get shared.

## How it fits your packaging rules

Truer doesn't mean softer packaging. Use the title formats (Titles deep dive) **and** put the true feeling in the first 30 seconds. Packaging gets the click. Recognition gets the share.

deep.title: The flywheel: the one loop your channel runs on
deep.dek: You said 'firewheel'. It's the flywheel, Jim Collins' idea that Amazon and most big creators run on. Here's yours.
sources: Jim Collins, Good to Great (2001) and Turning the Flywheel (2019)
Your Intro Lab and demand research
deep.md:
## What a flywheel is

A flywheel is a heavy wheel. The first push barely moves it. The tenth push moves it a bit. By the hundredth, it's spinning on its own momentum, and each push adds to the speed you already built.

Jim Collins used it in *Good to Great* (2001) to explain how good companies became great: **there was no single big moment**. From the inside it was one loop, pushed again and again, for years. Companies that failed did the opposite. They changed strategy every time something didn't work right away. He called that the **doom loop**.

## Amazon's version

Bezos drew it after meeting Collins: lower prices → more customers → more sellers → more products → lower costs → lower prices. Every arrow causes the next. That's the test of a real flywheel: **each step has to cause the next one**, not just happen near it.

## Ed's version for YouTube

Ed's emails describe it without using the word:

- Promote something in **every** video, so every video grows something (the list, the offer).
- Talk to your viewers 2-3 hours a day, because understanding them makes the next video better.
- Views per video matter more than subscribers, and money per view matters more than views.

## Yours, right now

Look at the diagram above. Your loop has five steps:

1. **An honest test video** (a real 60-day test, real measurements).
2. **The right viewers find it**: guys around 18 who want to look better without bro-science.
3. **They comment**: questions, doubts, "try X next".
4. **You get better ideas and proof**: the comments become your next titles, and your measured results become your thumbnails ('Day 1 vs Day 60').
5. **The next video is better**, so it travels further, and the loop turns faster.

The push that matters most is the one that moves the wheel every week: **uploading on a rhythm with promise-first packaging**. New tools, new apps, a new editing pack: those are polish on the wheel, not pushes.

## The outer ring (later)

Once the inner loop spins: an email list from your comments' best questions → one product or one honest sponsor that solves the same problem as the videos → money for an editor → more videos → faster loop. Ed's warning: one product, the simplest version first.

## How to use this

- Write your loop on one line and stick it above your desk.
- Before any new project, ask: **which arrow does this push?** If none, it's a hobby (fine, but call it that).
- Don't switch loops after one flop. Collins' doom loop is exactly that.

deep.title: Hooks: what the newsletters say vs what you measured
deep.dek: TubeLab's 3 outlier hooks, checked against your own Intro Lab data, plus a version of each for the gum video.
sources: Your Intro Lab findings (553 videos, 8 Nov 2026)
deep.md:
## What TubeLab found

They pulled the top outlier videos in many niches and read the first 30 seconds of each. Three hooks kept showing up:

- **Cold open.** Drop the viewer into one person's moment: a name, a place, a number. Then the twist.
- **"You" scenario.** Put the viewer inside a moment they know too well. Works best for money, health and fitness.
- **Bold claim.** One sentence that sounds wrong. The whole video proves it.

Plus one oddball that did 10x its channel average: *"Finish this sentence. I'll finally be happy when…"*

## What your own data says

Your Intro Lab measured hits vs flops across 553 videos (chart above). The pattern behind all three hooks is the same: **say what the viewer gets, fast, and make it feel easy**. Greeting-first and credentials-first openings lose badly, and no newsletter hook starts with "Hey guys".

What TubeLab doesn't tell you: a hook only works if the next 30 seconds pay it off. Your data says concrete steps (77% vs 33%) and escalation (85% vs 36%) are what keep people after the hook.

## Gum video versions (60 days of jawline gum)

**Cold open**
> Day 1. One piece of this gum felt like chewing a car tyre. Sixty days and about forty hours of chewing later, I put the same tape measure on my jaw.

**"You" scenario**
> You catch your side profile in a car window and your jaw just… isn't there. So you start chewing gum because a guy on TikTok said so.

**Bold claim**
> Chewing gum can't give you a jawline. Most of what you see under your ear is fat and posture, not muscle. So for 60 days, I tested the one part gum *can* change.

**Finish the sentence**
> Finish this sentence: I'd look better if my jaw was ___.

## Pick by the evidence

Use the bold claim when your result is honest and surprising. Use the cold open when your test has a dramatic day-1 moment on camera. Use the 'you' scenario when the problem is embarrassing and common. All three still need the promise in the first 10 seconds.

deep.title: How to read a study like Adam Mastroianni
deep.dek: Why most interventions 'do nothing', why one study is never enough, and a 5-question check for every looks claim you make.
sources: Adam Mastroianni, Experimental History, 'We need more goat sacrifices' (10 Nov 2026)
Peter Rossi, The Iron Law of Evaluation (1987)
deep.md:
## The Iron Law

In 1987 the sociologist Peter Rossi wrote a half-joking paper with rules everyone still quotes:

- **Iron Law:** the expected net effect of a big social program is zero.
- **Stainless Steel Law:** the better the evaluation, the more likely it finds no effect.
- **Brass Law:** the more a program tries to *change people*, the more likely it does nothing.

Mastroianni lists examples: $3 billion in US school grants with no clear effect; laptops for every child in Peru (a 10-year trial in 531 schools, zero effect on grades); messages meant to persuade parents to vaccinate that didn't work, and one that backfired.

## Why this matters for a looks channel

Your whole niche is people trying to *change themselves*: jaw, skin, bloat, posture. That's exactly what the Brass Law is about. So expect most hacks to do little, and treat big promises as suspicious until proven.

## "Rinky-dink interventions have rinky-dink effects"

Before psychology's replication crisis, people believed tiny tricks had big effects. When 100 psychology studies were re-run in 2015, only about a third of the significant results came out significant again. Mastroianni's rule of thumb: a small trick usually has a small effect, or none.

## Bad study, real effect

His favourite example is the 1975 "illusion of control" study. It's taught as "people value lottery tickets more if they pick the numbers", but it actually used football cards, and pickers simply chose their favourite players. Proper replications with real lotteries find nothing. Yet people blow on dice and wear lucky socks. **A study can be bad while the thing it describes is real.** That's a great script beat.

## Your 5-question check (put it in claims.md)

1. **One study or many?** A meta-analysis of trials beats one trial, which beats a mechanism ("it increases blood flow, so…").
2. **Was it pre-registered and did it have a control group?** If not, "worked" might mean nothing.
3. **How big, in real units?** "Significant" means little. Look for millimetres, hairs per cm², kg.
4. **Tiny trick, huge promise?** Rinky-dink alarm. Ask for more evidence.
5. **Who's selling it?** The hair-loss ad in your inbox is a perfect example: a real treatment, oversold.

## How to say it on camera

"Here's what the best evidence says, here's how big the effect is, and here's what I measured on myself." Honest null results ("this did nothing") are rare in your niche, and that's your edge.

deep.title: The taste gap: a 15-minute daily editing rep
deep.dek: rystal's loop, Ira Glass's 'gap' and Austin Kleon's 'steal like an artist', turned into a 4-week plan for Resolve.
sources: Austin Kleon, Steal Like an Artist (2012)
deep.md:
## The gap

Ira Glass (This American Life) has a famous point about beginners: you got into this because you have good taste, so for the first couple of years you can *see* your work isn't as good as you want. That gap is normal. The only way through is **volume**: make a lot of work, on a deadline.

rystal says the same from the other side: you can't edit better than what you've seen. If your feed is mid edits, mid feels like the ceiling.

## Steal like an artist

Austin Kleon's rule, which rystal follows: copy *concepts*, not work. You copy one move (the easing on a zoom, how a title builds, the timing of a cut), learn why it works, then mix three stolen moves into something that's yours. Copying a whole edit teaches nothing. Copying a move and taking it apart teaches everything.

## The loop

1. **Consume great work properly.** Not scrolling: one 10-second moment, frame by frame, replayed until you can say why it feels clean.
2. **Write one line**: "the text overshoots and settles in 6 frames".
3. **Make something in 15 minutes.** A text animation, a circle in Fusion, one zoom.

## 4-week plan

- **Week 1: Collect.** Pick 3 editors whose work embarrasses you (one in your niche, one motion designer, one documentary channel). Save 7 moments into a 'steal file' folder.
- **Week 2: Rebuild.** Each day, rebuild one saved moment in Resolve. Match it as closely as you can. Ugly is fine.
- **Week 3: Mix.** Combine two moves per day (for example, overshoot easing + your wojak entering).
- **Week 4: Ship.** Use your three best moves in your next video's intro. Compare its retention graph with your last one.

## Rules

- 15 minutes, every day, not 3 hours on Sunday. Small daily reps beat bursts.
- Always note **why** a move works. That note is the real skill.
- Keep everything you make, even bad ones. In 3 months, scrolling back is the best motivation there is.

deep.title: Minoxidil + microneedling: what the evidence actually says
deep.dek: The ad in your inbox, checked. What works for male pattern hair loss, how big the effect is, and how a video on it could look.
sources: Meta-analysis of 8 RCTs (472 people), Chinese Medicine and Natural Products 2024
deep.md:
## What the ad said

Tom Cruise (62) vs Jude Law (52): the younger man looks older because of his hairline. Then the Norwood scale, a personal story, "my doctor said it's fine", and a discount on a minoxidil + derma-pen kit that will let you "gain back much of what you've already lost".

## What the evidence says

- **Minoxidil** (topical, 5% for men) is one of only two treatments with long-standing approval for male pattern hair loss. The other is finasteride, which is prescription only. Mostly, minoxidil **slows loss and thickens existing hair**. Regrowth is partial, and the trials mostly looked at the crown, not the temples.
- **Adding microneedling helps.** A 2024 meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials (472 people) found more hair with microneedling + minoxidil than minoxidil alone. A 2025 meta-analysis found the same, with a large but very uneven effect between trials. A 2023 network analysis ranked minoxidil + microneedling first for hair density.
- **But:** the trials are small, the results vary a lot between them, and most last 3-6 months. Nobody has shown "regrow everything".

## What the ad left out

- A shed in the first weeks is common and scares people into quitting.
- It only works while you keep using it. Stop, and the gains fade over months.
- Microneedling done wrong (too deep, dirty needles) can irritate or infect the scalp.
- At 18, the first step is a doctor or dermatologist confirming it's pattern loss and not something else (stress, low iron, thyroid).

## The video idea

**"Losing your hair at 18: the only things with real evidence"**

- Hook: the Norwood scale on screen, "find your number" (a self-test, which your Intro Lab says gets replays).
- Body: what works (minoxidil, finasteride with a doctor, microneedling as an add-on), how big the effect is in real numbers, and what doesn't (most shampoos, most supplements unless you're actually deficient).
- Ending on value: a one-screen plan, "see a doctor first if you're under 20".

The ad's structure (comparison → self-check → story → offer) is copyable. Its promises aren't.

deep.title: Content for buyers: Ed's money ideas, filtered for an 18-year-old
deep.dek: What to take from 'the $240k video' and 'top earners make 20x per view' now, and what to save for later.
sources: Ed Lawrence emails: 'Copy this video' (12 Nov), '25 tough lessons' (5 Nov), 'niche views down 65%' (19 Oct), '100 nuggets' (13 Oct 2026)
deep.md:
## Ed's claims (his numbers, not verified)

- One video that gave away the free version of his paid system made **$240k in 90 days**, 2,000+ emails and 130k views.
- Of 198 channels he tracked, the **top 25% of earners got about the same views** as the bottom 25%, but made **~20x more per view**.
- In 42 of 44 niches for course creators, demand fell since 2023. **Self-improvement: -45%.**

All three come from the person selling the system that fixes them, so treat them as hints, not facts.

## What applies to you now

1. **The "free version" video is also a great binge video.** Lay out your whole method, step by step, with 1-3 simple actions per step. "This was so good I should have paid for it" is the feeling you want, sale or not.
2. **Mention the next step early.** He lost ~2,000 emails by plugging his list at minute 19 instead of the first 90 seconds. For you, the "next step" is your playlist or your next test video.
3. **Be specific, not "self-improvement".** If broad self-improvement demand is falling, specific, measurable looks topics are the safer place to be.
4. **Talk to viewers.** He spends 2-3 hours a day on it. You can reply to every comment while you're small. That's your demand research for free.

## What to save for later

- One product, simplest version first. No free community (it eats your time).
- Promote something in every video once you have something worth promoting.
- A "contentment number": decide what's enough before the money pulls you into grinding 24/7.

## Where I disagree with Ed

- "Hire an editor ASAP" and "short-form is a waste": his advice is for business owners with money. At your stage, editing *is* your skill-building, and Shorts are cheap tests of hooks.
- "Never use visual metaphors in thumbnails" is too absolute. Your Thumb Lab found clear outcome images win, which is a narrower rule.
